transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I’m Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

I’m here because… I know this is going to sound strange, but at work I keep hearing voices. Not just like a thought in my head — I mean clear, like somebody is standing right next to me talking.

It comes through the call-light speaker sometimes, and sometimes from the hallway vents. They’ll tell me which patient records have been changed. It’s specific, like they know exactly what was altered, and I’ll stop and listen because it sounds so real. But then the unit will be quiet, nobody else reacts, and when I ask or look around, nobody else seems to hear it.

It’s been really upsetting, because I work as a nursing assistant, so the call lights and the hallway sounds are things I’m used to. I know what they normally sound like. This isn’t just background noise or me mishearing a patient. It’s a voice, or voices, and it’s clear. That’s why I came in.

Have you ever felt like there are thoughts or ideas that others are putting into your mind, or that certain things happening around you are specifically directed at you? For example, do you feel like people are talking about you or plotting against you?

Yes… I mean, I don’t know if I’d say “putting thoughts in my mind,” exactly, but I do feel like certain things at work are aimed at me, or like I’m the one who’s seeing what everyone else is pretending not to see.

It’s mostly with the wound-care charts. I know there’s a pattern in them — like the way the entries line up, the changes in the documentation, the timing of it. It’s not random. And when I bring it up, my supervisor keeps saying it’s just late entries or coding mistakes, like I’m making too much out of it. But that doesn’t feel right. I can tell there’s something there that management doesn’t want people noticing.

And then once I caught it, it started feeling like they were watching what I write. Like if I document something too clearly, or if I mention the wrong detail, someone is going to come back through and check it because they know I saw the pattern. I know how that sounds, but I’m not just guessing. I work with those charts all the time. I know when something is off.
Have you ever felt that your thoughts are not entirely your own, like someone is inserting thoughts into your mind or controlling your thinking in some way?

I don’t really think of it that way, no. Like… I don’t have a sense of somebody reaching into my head and placing a thought there, if that’s what you mean. My thoughts still feel like mine, mostly.

Sometimes I’ll get stuck on something and it’s hard to let it go, and then I’ll wonder why I can’t stop thinking about it, but that feels different from someone controlling it. It’s more like my mind keeps circling back because something doesn’t feel right. So… no, I haven’t noticed thoughts being inserted into my mind or controlled exactly. I’m just trying to sort out what’s happening and whether I can trust what I’m noticing.
Do you ever feel like your thoughts are being broadcast out loud for others to hear, or that events or actions happening around you are directly related to you in a special or unusual way?

I don’t think my thoughts are being broadcast out loud, no. I don’t have that feeling like everyone can hear what I’m thinking.

But the other part… yes. That’s more what’s been happening. It feels like certain things around me at work are connected to me because I’m the one who noticed the pattern. Especially with the wound-care charts. I keep looking at the entries and the timing and the way some things are changed, and it’s just too lined up to be nothing. My supervisor keeps saying it’s late entries, or coding mistakes, or that I’m reading too much into it, but I know those charts. I work with them all the time. I can tell when something is off.

And once I caught it, it started feeling like management knows I caught it. Like they’re watching what I write now, checking my documentation, seeing if I put down the wrong detail or say too much. It’s not like I want to believe that, and I know it probably sounds extreme, but I can’t shake it. It feels directed at me because I’m the one who saw what they don’t want anyone else to see.
Have you ever felt that certain events, gestures, or conversations you observe are secretly about you or meant to communicate something directly to you?

Yes… that’s probably the closest way to describe it. Not like every conversation in the hallway is about me, but certain things at work feel like they’re not just normal background stuff anymore.

With the wound-care charts, it feels like there’s a message in the way the documentation is being handled — the timing of the entries, what gets changed, what gets left vague. I know it sounds like I’m reading into paperwork, but I’ve worked with those charts long enough to know what routine mistakes look like, and this doesn’t feel routine. It feels like there’s a pattern management doesn’t want anyone to see.

And then when my supervisor brushes it off and says, “Oh, those are just late entries,” or “That’s probably coding errors,” it almost feels like that response itself is part of it, like they’re trying to steer me away from looking too closely. After I noticed it, I started feeling like they were paying attention to what I write, like my documentation is being watched because I’m the one who caught it. So yes, in that sense, it does feel directed at me — like the whole thing is about what I noticed and whether I’ll say too much.

Do you ever feel like certain things that happen, even if they seem ordinary to others, have a special meaning or connection to you personally—like they were meant to send you a message or reveal something hidden?

Yes. I mean… yes, that’s what it feels like with the charts. Other people keep acting like it’s ordinary paperwork stuff, like late entries or coding mistakes or someone just being sloppy, but to me it doesn’t feel random. I know those wound-care charts. I look at them all the time. I know what normal mistakes look like, and this is different.

It’s the timing, the way certain things are changed, the way some parts are left vague. It’s like the pattern is there if you’re actually paying attention, and I’m the one who caught it. And when my supervisor says, “No, it’s nothing,” or tries to explain it away, that almost makes it feel more obvious, because it feels like they don’t want me looking at it too closely.

So yes, certain ordinary things at work feel like they’re connected to me now. Like management knows I noticed, and they’re watching what I write in my own documentation, checking if I say too much or put something down that shows what’s really going on. I know that probably sounds like a lot, but I can’t just ignore it. It feels like the charts are revealing something hidden, and because I saw it, now it’s aimed at me too.

Have you ever felt that certain actions or events, like changes in documentation or conversations, are not just about you but are specifically meant to communicate a message directly to you, beyond what you've already described?

Yes… I think so, but it’s hard to separate from what I already said because to me it’s all part of the same thing.

It’s not like I hear an actual voice or something saying, “This is for you.” It’s more that the way the documentation changes feels like it’s signaling something. Like when certain wound-care entries are adjusted, or when something is entered late, or when the wording is just vague enough that no one could easily question it — it feels too specific. It feels like the charts are showing a pattern, and that pattern is almost… I don’t know, like it’s revealing what they’re trying to keep hidden.

And then when I bring it up and my supervisor says it’s just late entries or coding mistakes, I can’t accept that as a normal explanation anymore. I know what those charts usually look like. I know the difference between regular sloppiness and something that’s being covered over. So when they dismiss me that quickly, it feels like that’s a message too — like, “Stop looking. Don’t write anything that points to this. Don’t make trouble.”

And I feel like they’re watching my own notes now because I’m the one who caught it. Like they’re checking what I write to see if I’m going to put down too much or connect the wrong pieces out loud. So yes, I guess it does feel like some of it is directed at me personally, not just happening around me. It feels like I noticed what I wasn’t supposed to notice, and now the way people respond and the way the charts keep changing is telling me that.
Have you ever felt that your actions, like what you write or say, are being controlled by an outside force or that someone is trying to influence what you do without your permission?

I don’t know if I’d say controlled, exactly. That word feels… stronger than what I mean. I don’t feel like my hand is being moved for me or like something takes over my body and makes me write things. It’s still me writing, it’s still me choosing my words.

But influenced? Pressured? Maybe. I do feel like I second-guess what I put down because I’m aware of how it might be looked at, or how certain people might react if I document something too clearly. So I’ll sit there thinking, “If I write it this way, are they going to say I’m making a problem? If I leave it vague, am I protecting myself or am I letting something slide?” It gets in my head.

So no, not an outside force controlling me like that. More like I feel watched and pushed to be careful, and that makes me change how I say things sometimes. But I still know it’s me making the decision.

Have you ever felt that something in your environment — like a real sound you heard or something you saw — had a hidden meaning or was meant specifically for you to notice, even though others might not understand that meaning?

Yes… especially at work. It’s not like, um, a random noise on the street or something where I think every little thing is about me. It’s more specific than that. It’s the charts, the documentation, the way things show up or get changed.

Like I’ll see a wound-care entry that’s been adjusted, or something entered late, or wording that’s just vague enough that it could slide past if you weren’t really looking. And to someone else, I know they’d say, “That’s normal, that happens, people chart late, people make coding errors.” But when I see it, it feels like it’s there for me to notice, because I know those records. I know the usual mistakes. This feels patterned.

And then when I ask about it and my supervisor says it’s nothing, that doesn’t settle it for me. It almost makes it feel more like there’s something underneath it. Like management doesn’t want anyone to see the pattern, and because I caught it, now they’re watching what I put in my own notes. So yes, I guess I do feel like certain things I’m seeing in the environment — the charts, the edits, the timing — have a meaning other people either don’t understand or don’t want to admit is there.

Have you ever felt that something you read, saw, or heard—like something in a chart or a message at work—was specifically meant for you to understand in a way that no one else could, almost like a secret code or message just for you?

Yes… that’s pretty much how it feels, although I don’t know if I would call it a “code” exactly. It’s not like numbers or symbols or something written in a cipher. It’s more that when I read the wound-care charts, I can see the pattern in them in a way other people either can’t see or won’t admit.

Like, one late entry by itself, fine. A vague note by itself, maybe that’s just sloppy charting. A coding mistake here and there, yes, I know that happens. I’ve worked around documentation long enough to know people make mistakes. But when the same kind of thing keeps happening around the same wound-care issues, and the wording keeps being adjusted just enough to make things less clear, and then the timing of the entries doesn’t line up cleanly… to me, that is not random. It reads like something is being shaped.

And when I try to explain that, my supervisor just says it’s late entries or coding mistakes, like I’m supposed to just drop it. But that answer feels too easy. It feels like they want me to stop looking at it, because I caught something I wasn’t supposed to catch. So yes, when I see those chart changes, I feel like I’m understanding something underneath the normal documentation that other people aren’t acknowledging.

And now I also feel like they’re watching what I write because of it. Like they know I’m the one who noticed, and they’re checking whether I’m going to document too much or connect the pieces too clearly. So it does feel personal in that way — not like a secret message with my name on it, but like the charts are showing me a pattern management doesn’t want anyone to see.

Outside of your workplace situation, have you ever had any experiences where you felt that there was a larger hidden plan, organization, or force involved in what you were noticing—something beyond just your workplace, like a government group, a secret network, or something that would not be easily verifiable by others?

No… I mean, not really in the sense of a government group or some secret organization outside of work. I’m not saying there’s some big national thing or people I’ve never met sending messages. That’s not what I mean.

What I’m talking about is the workplace, the wound-care charts, the management side of things. That’s where it feels real to me. I know those records, and I know when something is just a normal late entry or a simple mistake, and this doesn’t feel like that. It feels like there’s a pattern in the documentation that management doesn’t want anyone to see.

And when my supervisor keeps saying it’s just coding errors or people charting late, I know that’s the explanation they want me to accept, but it doesn’t fit with what I’m seeing. The wording changes, the timing, the way certain things are vague right where they shouldn’t be vague… it adds up.

So no, I’m not saying it’s the government or some secret network. But I do feel like the people at work know I caught something, and now they’re watching what I write because they don’t want me documenting it too clearly. That part feels very personal to me.

Outside of your concerns about the wound-care charts and your workplace, have you ever had any other experiences where you felt like there was a hidden pattern or meaning in something that others didn’t seem to notice?

Outside of work? No, not really. I mean… I don’t walk around thinking everything has some hidden meaning. It’s not like I see things on TV or hear songs or anything like that and think they’re meant for me. That’s not what this is.

It’s really tied to the wound-care charts and what’s happening there. That’s where the pattern is. I know it probably sounds like I keep coming back to the same thing, but that’s because that’s where I can actually see it. The late entries, the little wording changes, the coding mistakes that keep getting explained away — those are the things that don’t sit right with me. And when my supervisor says, “Oh, it’s just charting late,” or “That’s just a coding error,” I understand that’s what they want me to believe, but it doesn’t explain why it keeps lining up the way it does.

So no, outside of that, I can’t really think of another area where I feel like there’s some hidden meaning. But with the charts, yes. I know they’re showing something management doesn’t want anyone to see, and I feel like because I noticed it, they’re paying attention to what I write now. Like they’re watching my documentation to see if I’m going to spell it out too clearly.

Have you ever had times when you strongly believed something was true, even though others told you there was no evidence for it, and it wasn’t something most people would believe under the same circumstances?

Yes. I mean… yes, I guess that’s exactly what this is, if you put it that way.

With the wound-care charts, I know other people keep saying there isn’t proof, or that I’m reading too much into it. My supervisor especially keeps saying it’s just late entries, or coding mistakes, or people not charting clearly because they’re busy. And I understand those things can happen. I’m not saying every single late note means something by itself. But when it keeps happening around the same issues, and the wording changes just enough, and the timing doesn’t make sense, it stops feeling accidental.

Other people act like I should just accept the simple explanation, but I can’t, because I can see the pattern. It’s like the records are showing something management doesn’t want anyone to see. And the more I notice it, the more I feel like they know I noticed. Like now they’re watching what I write, checking my documentation, waiting to see if I’m going to connect it too clearly.

So yes, even when people tell me there’s no evidence, I still believe it. Because to me, the evidence is in the way the charts line up. It’s not one thing — it’s all the little things together.
Have you ever believed something was happening or true that you know most people would say is completely impossible or not based in reality, like something out of a fantasy or science fiction story?

No, not like fantasy or science fiction. I’m not saying anything impossible like that. I don’t believe there are aliens or mind control or anything that couldn’t happen in the real world.

What I’m talking about is something that could happen, and honestly does happen in places where people are trying to protect themselves — records being adjusted, language being softened, things being documented late so it looks different than it really was. That’s not science fiction to me. That’s paperwork. That’s management. That’s healthcare documentation.

I know other people might say I’m taking it too far, or that I’m seeing a pattern where there isn’t one, but I don’t think it’s impossible. I think the wound-care charts are showing something they don’t want anyone to see. And when my supervisor keeps brushing it off as late entries or coding mistakes, it just feels like she’s trying to get me to ignore what’s right in front of me.

And the part that really bothers me is that once I noticed it, I could tell they started paying attention to what I write. Like they’re watching my documentation now because I’m the one who caught it. So no, I wouldn’t call it fantasy. I would call it something people don’t want to admit is happening.
Have you ever felt that something or someone outside of your workplace was influencing events in your life or sending you messages in a way that others don't seem to understand?

No… not outside of the workplace. At least, not that I can think of. I don’t feel like strangers on the street are sending me messages, or that something outside is controlling things in my life. It’s not like that.

It really stays with the charts and the documentation. That’s the part that keeps bothering me, because it’s not vague to me. It’s not some random feeling from nowhere. I see it in the wound-care notes — the timing, the wording, the way things get entered late and then explained away as coding errors or normal charting problems. My supervisor keeps telling me that’s all it is, but I just don’t believe that explains the whole thing.

And once I noticed it, that’s when I started feeling like they were watching what I write more closely. Not “someone outside” sending me messages, but management, people connected to the documentation. Like they know I caught the pattern and now they’re checking my notes to see if I’m going to make it too obvious.

So if you mean outside of work, no. But with the wound-care charts, yes — I know there’s something there that they don’t want seen.

Have there been times when you believed something strongly, even when others couldn’t see it or prove it, but everything else in your life—like your thinking, your senses, or how you act—still felt normal and clear to you?

Yes… that’s probably the best way to describe it. Because outside of that, I don’t feel confused or out of touch with everything. I feel like I’m thinking clearly. I go through my day, I know what I’m doing, I know who people are, I know where I am. It’s not like everything feels unreal or like I’m not myself.

But with the wound-care charts, I know what I’m seeing. That’s the part I can’t just let go of. Other people keep acting like because they can’t “prove” it the way they want, then I’m supposed to ignore it. My supervisor keeps saying it’s just late entries, or coding mistakes, or normal charting issues, and I understand those things happen in healthcare. I really do. I’ve worked around documentation long enough to know people chart late, people use the wrong wording, things get cleaned up after the fact.

But this is different. It lines up too much. The timing, the way certain things are phrased, the way the explanations shift — it feels like the charts are showing a pattern management doesn’t want anyone to see. And I know people tell me I’m the only one seeing it, but that doesn’t make it disappear for me.

And then once I caught on to it, I could tell they were paying closer attention to me. Like what I write, how I document things, whether I’m going to put something in there that makes the pattern too clear. So yes, I believe it strongly even when other people say they can’t see it. But everything else feels normal to me. I don’t feel mixed up. I feel like I’m clear — maybe more clear about this than other people want me to be.

doctor.intent: Identify the patient's chief complaint or reason for seeking help
doctor.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I’m Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: I'm here because I keep hearing voices from the call-light speaker and the hallway vents telling me which patient records have been changed, clear as somebody standing next to me, even when the unit is quiet and nobody else hears it.
target_item.reason: This is the first reply of the consultation, so I must return the chief complaint symptom code.

patient.answer:
I’m here because… I know this is going to sound strange, but at work I keep hearing voices. Not just like a thought in my head — I mean clear, like somebody is standing right next to me talking.

It comes through the call-light speaker sometimes, and sometimes from the hallway vents. They’ll tell me which patient records have been changed. It’s specific, like they know exactly what was altered, and I’ll stop and listen because it sounds so real. But then the unit will be quiet, nobody else reacts, and when I ask or look around, nobody else seems to hear it.

It’s been really upsetting, because I work as a nursing assistant, so the call lights and the hallway sounds are things I’m used to. I know what they normally sound like. This isn’t just background noise or me mishearing a patient. It’s a voice, or voices, and it’s clear. That’s why I came in.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences delusions or fixed false beliefs in addition to auditory hallucinations, which would help differentiate between schizophrenia (F20.x) and other psychotic disorders.
doctor.question: Have you ever felt like there are thoughts or ideas that others are putting into your mind, or that certain things happening around you are specifically directed at you? For example, do you feel like people are talking about you or plotting against you?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know the wound-care charts are showing a pattern management doesn't want anyone to see, and even when my supervisor says it's just late entries or coding mistakes, I can tell they're watching what I write because I'm the one who caught it.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with persistent, non-bizarre delusions centered around workplace documentation, specifically wound-care charts, without other prominent psychotic symptoms or mood episodes. The delusional themes are non-persecutory in nature but involve a belief in a concealed pattern being manipulated by management, with associated concern about being monitored. There is no evidence of hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized or catatonic behavior, or significant functional decline outside the context of the delusional system. The presentation is consistent with Delusional Disorder, of the non-bizarre, non-odd type, without features of schizophrenia or brief psychotic disorder.
